Below is a concise, evidence-backed overview of how to estimate reliability in multicomponent stress–strength systems, with definitions, estimator classes, and architectural cases.

1) Definitions and model forms
- In the basic stress–strength model, reliability is R = P(X > Y), where X is strength and Y is stress; failure occurs when stress exceeds strength at any time, a concept widely used in mechanical reliability and many applied fields <cite id="4fbe3d7a-2">The “stress-strength” reliability can be described as an assessment of reliability of a component in terms of a random stress Y and a strength X; if Y > X then the system will fail, so R = P(X > Y) was introduced by Birnbaum and developed by Birnbaum and McCarty</cite>. 
- Multicomponent generalizations replace the single component minimum by order statistics. Canonical series/cold-standby formulations define system reliability as the probability that at least one component survives the common stress, i.e., R = P(X_{(k)} > Y) where X_{(k)} is the kth order statistic of component strengths under a common stress Y; equivalently, R = P(Y < min(X1,...,Xk)) or R = P(X_{k+1} < min(X1,...,Xk)) for a (k+1)th component comparison, with many authors parameterizing (X1,...,Xk+1) under independent gamma/Weibull/Pareto or exponential families <cite id="4fbe3d7a-0">Hanagal estimated system reliability R = P(X_{k+1} < min(X1,...,Xk)) when strengths X1,...,Xk and common stress X_{k+1} follow independent gamma or Weibull or Pareto; Pandit and Kantu considered parallel and series systems with exponential strength and stress; s-out-of-k systems were first developed by Bhattacharyya and Johnson and have broad applications</cite><cite id="4fbe3d7a-2">An s-out-of-k system functions if s or more of k statistically independent and identically distributed components withstand a common stress; this structure generalizes series and parallel systems</cite><cite id="2f5b5454-0">Hanagal obtained estimation for a series system under multivariate Pareto strengths with exponential common stress; for k components, he also treated parallel/series with two-parameter exponential; for dependent components, he estimated R = P(X_{k+1} < min(X1,...,Xk)) for independent X1,...,X_{k+1} under gamma/Weibull/Pareto; Ebrahimi discussed series models with bivariate Marshall–Olkin exponential strengths under q independent exponential stresses</cite><cite id="2f5b5454-4">For independent Y (stress) and X1,...,Xk (strengths), the multicomponent stress–strength reliability is expressed via order statistics of the strengths, and special cases include Weibull and multivariate exponential strengths with exponential stress; MLEs and MVUEs have been derived in such settings</cite>. 
- Beyond simple series/parallel, k-out-of-n and parallel–series architectures arise in critical systems; k-out-of-n requires s of k components to survive a common stress, while parallel–series combines subsystems in parallel with components in series, and flexible inference methods and ACI procedures have been developed for such structures <cite id="2f5b5454-2">Reliability inference of k-out-of-n systems under multicomponent stress–strength Burr–XII strengths has been studied; parallel–series systems combine parallel and series arrangements and are vital in power grids and aerospace; approximate confidence intervals and optimization designs exist for such systems; assuming independence of stress and strength is often unrealistic, motivating dependence-aware methods</cite>.

2) Single-component estimation: frequentist methods and intervals
- The single-component target R = P(X > Y) is widely estimated via maximum likelihood when X and Y are independent and follow common reliability families (exponential, Weibull, generalized exponential, Pareto, normal/gamma/Weibull mixtures). Numerous studies compare MLE with Bayesian alternatives, and highlight that other frequentist methods (least squares, spacings, Cramér–von Mises/Anderson–Darling) can outperform MLE in small samples <cite id="ff6d9445-0">Since Birnbaum, estimation of R = P(Y < X) has been widely studied; authors have used maximum likelihood and Bayesian methods under various life-testing schemes; many works focus on Weibull and generalized exponential families</cite><cite id="ff6d9445-2">For independent Weibull X and Y with equal shape, ten frequentist estimators were compared (MLE, least squares, weighted least squares, percentile, maximum product of spacing, minimum spacing distances, Cramér–von Mises, Anderson–Darling, Right-tail AD), with two parametric bootstrap intervals; simulation and a real data set showed MLE and product-of-spacings often minimize RMSE and interval length, especially in small samples</cite><cite id="ff6d9445-3">The percentile and maximum product-of-spacings methods were highly competitive across small and large samples for R estimation with equal Weibull shape; bias-corrected percentile bootstrap intervals were shortest on average</cite><cite id="ff6d9445-4">Comprehensive reviews (e.g., Kotz et al.) summarize single-component stress–strength estimation; specific studies cover exponential, Weibull (same or different shapes), and derive asymptotic MLEs and bootstrap intervals; Bayesian point and interval estimators are available for exponential stress–strength models based on recorded values</cite>. 
- Confidence intervals can be constructed via likelihood ratio, score, or bootstrap; record-value setups and Weibull stress–strength models have explicit Bayes and MLE estimators with bias/MSE studies and HPD intervals <cite id="ff6d9445-1">For stress–strength reliability based on record values from the Weibull distribution, Bayes and MLE estimators with squared error loss were derived, with bias and MSE studied; likelihood-based confidence intervals and bootstrap intervals (percentile and bias-corrected) and highest posterior density intervals were developed and compared via simulation</cite>. 
- In practical single-component inference under censoring, parametric families (exponential, Lindley, Burr XII, etc.) admit MLEs, consistent unbiased estimators, and Bayesian/MC intervals; progressive Type-II censoring and bootstrap are commonly used <cite id="ff6d9445-4">Under progressive Type I censoring, MLEs for single-component stress–strength models were obtained and asymptotic and bootstrap intervals derived for double-parameter Burr XII; consistent UMV unbiased, MLE, Bayesian, and bootstrap methods were used for Lindley stress–strength models</cite>. 
- For specific parametric families (e.g., Weibull–Rayleigh), joint likelihood can still be optimized: MLE and approximate MLE are derived and validated on real data <cite id="2f5b5454-1">For independent Weibull–Rayleigh X and Y, MLE and approximate MLE of the stress–strength reliability are obtained; two real-data applications demonstrate flexibility</cite>.

3) Single-component estimation: Bayesian formulations
- Bayesian formulations place priors on the distribution parameters of X and Y (or on R directly) and infer posterior modes/means and credible intervals; models include exponential, Weibull (equal or different shapes), generalized families, and mixed/record-value sampling schemes <cite id="ff6d9445-1">Bayes estimator (squared error loss) and MLE derived for Weibull stress–strength reliability from record values; simulation compares bias/MSE and interval coverage properties</cite><cite id="ff6d9445-4">Bayesian methods have been applied for exponential stress–strength models based on recorded values; for Weibull with same shape, asymptotic MLEs and bootstrap intervals are discussed; Lindley families admit consistent unbiased, MLE, Bayesian, and bootstrap estimation</cite>. 
- Modern hierarchical forms such as “unit-generated” Weibull (UGG–Weibull) allow different generator parameters for strength and stress sharing a common Weibull baseline; fully Bayesian inference with informative priors yields posterior sampling and credible intervals for the reliability R_{s,k} under progressive Type-II censoring <cite id="4fbe3d7a-4">A fully Bayesian framework estimates multicomponent stress–strength reliability R_{s,k} under a UGG–Weibull model where strength X and stress Y share a common Weibull baseline with shape λ and scale θ but have generator parameters (α1,β1,μ1) and (α2,β2,μ2); the eight-dimensional parameter vector is ϕ = (α1,β1,μ1,α2,β2,μ2,λ,θ)</cite>.

4) Multicomponent architectures: series cold-standby, parallel, and k-out-of-n
- Series (cold-standby) systems: system reliability R = P(Y < X_{(k)}), equivalently R = P(X_{k+1} < min(X1,...,Xk)) for an additional component; estimation under independent strengths and common stress has been treated for exponential, gamma, Weibull, Pareto families, and for dependent strengths via multivariate Pareto/multivariate exponential models <cite id="4fbe3d7a-0">R = P(X_{k+1} < min(X1,...,Xk)) with independent X1,...,Xk+1 under gamma/Weibull/Pareto; exponential series/parallel were studied by Pandit and Kantu; s-out-of-k systems and their applications are surveyed</cite><cite id="2f5b5454-0">Hanagal estimated series reliability under multivariate Pareto strengths with exponential stress; for parallel/series with two-parameter exponential strengths and stress, estimators were derived; for non-independent components, a bivariate exponential model for two components with common stress was considered; under Marshall–Olkin exponential strengths, series models with multiple independent exponential stresses were analyzed</cite><cite id="2f5b5454-4">MLE and MVUE estimators were derived for R = P(Y < X_{(k)}) with Weibull stress and Weibull strengths with same or unknown scale and known shape; multivariate exponential strengths with exponential stress have also been considered</cite>. 
- Parallel systems: R = P(Y < X_{(1)}), i.e., the stress must be less than the smallest strength; classical estimators exist under exponential and Weibull families, and s-out-of-k generalizations have been studied extensively <cite id="4fbe3d7a-0">Pandit and Kantu estimated multicomponent stress–strength reliability for parallel and series systems under exponential strength and stress</cite><cite id="4fbe3d7a-2">Parallel and series systems are special cases of k-out-of-n; s-out-of-k systems were first formalized by Bhattacharyya and Johnson and used in industrial/military contexts</cite><cite id="2f5b5454-4">Independent-strengths/Weibull models provide explicit expressions and estimators for parallel/series reliability</cite>. 
- k-out-of-n and mixed structures: R is expressed via order statistics or inclusion-exclusion over combinations, with estimators available under specific strength/stress families (e.g., Burr–XII) and progressively censored samples; parallel–series architectures combine these and have dedicated inference procedures and approximate confidence intervals <cite id="2f5b5454-2">Burr–XII-based k-out-of-n reliability in multicomponent stress–strength models has been estimated; parallel–series systems combine series and parallel at multiple levels and appear in power and aerospace; approximate confidence intervals and optimization designs exist; dependence between stress and strength is often realistic and should be modeled</cite><cite id="4fbe3d7a-0">Estimation for s-out-of-k systems has been extensively investigated for log-logistic, generalized exponential, Rayleigh, Burr Type XII, generalized Rayleigh, and Weibull/bivariate Kumarswamy cases</cite>. 
- General coherent structures: For arbitrary minimal cut-set/structure functions, reliability can be written as expectations over ordered strengths, enabling unified likelihood construction and numerical optimization; examples include Eryilmaz’s results for general coherent systems and for systems with dependent elements within units <cite id="2f5b5454-4">Eryilmaz studied stress–strength reliability for general coherent systems and for systems with n independent components each consisting of m dependent elements; Jae & Eun and Hanagal provided MLEs and MVUEs for specific coherent structures under Weibull and multivariate exponential models</cite>.

5) Advanced and dependent models
- Dependent strengths and stresses: Early work models multivariate exponential strengths (absolutely continuous or Marshall–Olkin) with independent or dependent stresses; more recent work explicitly incorporates dependence between stress and strength via copulas and multivariate families, which improves realism in environmental/operational settings <cite id="2f5b5454-0">Ebrahimi discussed series stress–strength models with bivariate Marshall–Olkin exponential strengths under independent exponential stresses; Hanagal treated dependent parallel systems with bivariate exponential strengths and common stress</cite><cite id="2f5b5454-2">Dependence between stress and strength is often induced by shared factors; parallel–series reliability studies emphasize that independence assumptions may be unrealistic, motivating dependence-aware estimation</cite>. 
- Copula-based and mixed-structure estimation: Copula frameworks and parallel–series decompositions allow flexible marginal modeling (e.g., Weibull, Rayleigh) with dependence captured by Hoeffding–Sklar copulas; inference uses MLE in the joint likelihood, bootstrap intervals, and Bayesian posterior sampling <cite id="ff6d9445-4">Stress–strength reliability has been studied under copula-based setups and progressively censored bivariate samples; methods include MLE, bootstrap intervals, and Bayesian estimation across exponential, Lindley, and Burr families</cite><cite id="2f5b5454-2">Copula-based reliability estimation has been applied to parallel–series systems in multicomponent stress–strength dependent models, enabling modular reliability aggregation with dependence</cite>. 
- Competing stresses or multiple stresses: Extensions estimate R for systems under multiple stresses with dependence, e.g., n stresses on k components arranged parallel or series; estimation proceeds by defining system failure events and optimizing the joint likelihood under multivariate exponential/Weibull families <cite id="2f5b5454-0">The article considers k components under n stresses with components arranged parallel or series, relaxing independence across stresses and accommodating dependence structures</cite>. 
- Load-sharing and dependent strengths within units: When components inside a unit share load (load-sharing), strength is a function of surviving components; Eryilmaz’s formulations address stress–strength reliability when n independent components each have m dependent elements, enabling estimation with MLE and MVUE under Weibull/exponential-type models <cite id="2f5b5454-4">Stress–strength reliability for systems with n independent components each consisting of m dependent elements was considered by Eryilmaz, with MLE and MVUE available; such load-sharing/dependent-element structures appear in engine, power, communication, and tire systems</cite>.

6) Data schemes, asymptotics, and intervals (practical tools)
- MLE is the default frequentist estimator when a closed-form likelihood exists; under regularity conditions, asymptotic normality of MLEs yields approximate confidence intervals via Fisher information, but simulations often show spacings-based and percentile/bias-corrected bootstrap intervals perform better in coverage and interval length for small to moderate samples <cite id="ff6d9445-2">For independent Weibull strengths and stresses, MLE and product-of-spacings were among top performers in RMSE and interval length; bias-corrected percentile bootstrap intervals were shortest on average</cite><cite id="ff6d9445-3">Percentile and maximum product-of-spacings methods were highly competitive across sample sizes; two parametric bootstrap intervals were compared</cite>. 
- Record-value and progressively censored schemes are common in reliability; estimators and intervals have been developed for these sampling schemes across exponential/Weibull/Burr families, using likelihood-ratio/score intervals and bootstrap <cite id="ff6d9445-1">Record-based Weibull stress–strength models admit MLE and Bayes estimators with bias/MSE analyses and likelihood/score/bootstrap confidence intervals plus HPD credible sets</cite><cite id="ff6d9445-4">Under progressive Type-II censoring, MLEs, asymptotic intervals, and bootstrap intervals have been derived for Burr XII; Lindley families admit consistent unbiased, MLE, Bayesian, and bootstrap estimation</cite>. 
- Specialized distributions and mixtures (e.g., generalized exponential/log-logistic/Rayleigh, Weibull–Rayleigh) support closed-form or numerically tractable likelihoods; approximate MLEs and simulation studies validate performance on real data <cite id="4fbe3d7a-0">Estimation under log-logistic, generalized exponential, Rayleigh, Burr Type XII, generalized Rayleigh, and Weibull/bivariate Kumarswamy families has been developed for multicomponent stress–strength models</cite><cite id="2f5b5454-1">Weibull–Rayleigh stress–strength reliability admits MLE and approximate MLE; two real data applications are provided</cite><cite id="ff6d9445-0">Generalized exponential and Weibull stress–strength reliability have been estimated via MLE and Bayesian methods with extensive reviews</cite>. 
- Unified likelihood and numerical optimization: For general coherent structures and s-out-of-k reliability expressed through order statistics, numerically stable likelihood evaluation with profile likelihood or EM-style algorithms yields point estimates and profile-based confidence intervals; Bayesian MCMC can sample the joint posterior over parameters and reliability <cite id="2f5b5454-4">Order-statistics expressions for multicomponent reliability enable MLE and MVUE under Weibull and multivariate exponential models; general coherent systems and dependent-element units have explicit estimators</cite><cite id="4fbe3d7a-4">Fully Bayesian estimation with UGG–Weibull strength/stress parameters can be implemented via joint posterior sampling over the eight-dimensional parameter vector</cite>.

7) Practical guidance and model selection
- Start by mapping the physical system to a reliability event: series/cold-standby uses the minimum strength exceeding stress; k-out-of-n uses the s-th order statistic threshold; parallel uses the maximum strength threshold; complex systems decompose into parallel–series or general coherent structures. Then select a family that fits stress and strength marginals (exponential/Weibull for monotone hazard, generalized families for heavy tails), and consider dependence via copulas if stress and strength are influenced by shared covariates or mechanisms <cite id="4fbe3d7a-2">System failure when stress exceeds the minimum component strength motivates series/cold-standby; s-out-of-k generalizes this; R = P(X > Y) is the single-component prototype</cite><cite id="2f5b5454-0">Hanagal and Ebrahimi’s treatments cover series/parallel/k-out-of-n under exponential, gamma/Weibull/Pareto, and multivariate exponential/Weibull families with and without dependence</cite><cite id="2f5b5454-2">Parallel–series architectures are widely used in critical infrastructure; dependence between stress and strength should be modeled when realistic</cite>. 
- Frequentist workhorse: MLE under the joint likelihood for the chosen family; compute profile likelihood or bootstrap intervals if closed-form quantiles are unavailable; favor product-of-spacings or percentile/bias-corrected bootstrap when samples are small and MLE is slightly biased <cite id="ff6d9445-2">MLE and product-of-spacings were top performers for R with independent Weibull strengths and stress</cite><cite id="ff6d9445-3">Bias-corrected percentile bootstrap yielded shorter intervals than percentile alone</cite>. 
- Bayesian approach: specify priors on shape/scale and any dependence parameters; use MCMC or variational methods to sample R or its logit; obtain credible intervals and model-averaged predictions; useful when prior information (e.g., design standards) is strong or data are limited <cite id="ff6d9445-1">Bayes and MLE for Weibull record-based stress–strength with interval comparisons via simulation</cite><cite id="4fbe3d7a-4">UGG–Weibull fully Bayesian framework estimates R_{s,k} with a joint posterior over generator and baseline Weibull parameters</cite>. 
- Sensitivity analysis and diagnostics: compare MLE, spacings, and Bayesian estimators under progressive censoring and record sampling; check coverage of intervals via simulation; assess robustness to misspecification by fitting generalized exponential instead of Weibull, or by adding a Gaussian copula to capture tail dependence <cite id="ff6d9445-2">Simulation and real data comparisons guide estimator and interval selection for R under Weibull</cite><cite id="ff6d9445-4">Across exponential, Lindley, and Burr families, MLE, bootstrap, and Bayesian methods have been benchmarked; progressive censoring settings are covered</cite><cite id="2f5b5454-2">Copula-based dependence-aware estimation improves realism and supports parallel–series aggregation</cite>. 
- Case library: s-out-of-k in power and telecom; engine/vehicle thermal-mechanical systems; multi-unit turbines or pumps; parallel–series power grids; wind farm turbine clusters. Each maps to an R expression in terms of order statistics and strengths/stresses; parameter estimation follows the general recipes above <cite id="2f5b5454-4">Examples include 4-out-of-8 engines, power stations with 6/8 units online, communication systems with 6/10 transmitters, and 6/8 tires; s-out-of-k is reviewed by Kuo & Zuo</cite>. 

8) Summary of estimation pipelines
- Specify the system reliability expression R as an order-statistic probability P(Y < X_{(s)}), or a coherent-structure expectation; choose joint likelihood under appropriate marginals (e.g., Weibull, exponential, generalized families) and dependence structure (independence or copula/multivariate exponential); collect data (full, record, or progressively censored); then:
  - Frequentist: compute MLE (possibly profile), evaluate asymptotic variances or simulate bootstrap intervals; consider product-of-spacings and AD/CV MLE variants; benchmark RMSE and coverage on simulated data before applying to the field sample <cite id="ff6d9445-2">Ten frequentist estimators and two bootstrap intervals for R under Weibull with comparisons via simulation and a real data set</cite><cite id="ff6d9445-3">Product-of-spacings and bias-corrected bootstrap often yield best RMSE and interval lengths</cite><cite id="ff6d9445-1">Likelihood-based and bootstrap intervals with Bayes/MSE comparisons for Weibull record-based R</cite>. 
  - Bayesian: place priors on all parameters (shape/scale for marginals, dependence parameters, baseline Weibull if using UGG–Weibull); run MCMC to sample the joint posterior; compute posterior means/modes for R and credible intervals; use importance sampling or Laplace approximations for faster computation in simpler models <cite id="4fbe3d7a-4">UGG–Weibull model defines a joint eight-dimensional parameter space; fully Bayesian estimation yields R_{s,k} posteriors</cite><cite id="ff6d9445-1">Squared-error Bayes estimators and HPD intervals are available with performance diagnostics</cite>. 
- Validate with cross-validated predictive checks (e.g., survival probability of a hold-out sample of stresses/strengths) and perform sensitivity analysis over priors and distributions; prefer models that pass safety-margin checks and yield conservative credible upper bounds when regulatory decision-making is involved <cite id="ff6d9445-4">Reviews and applications across exponential/Weibull/Burr families emphasize validation on real data</cite><cite id="2f5b5454-2">Dependence-aware estimation and parallel–series modeling support realistic predictions for critical systems</cite>.

Title: On estimation procedures of stress-strength reliability for Weibull distribution with application
Snippet: Since the pioneering work of Birnbaum [1], the statistical inference of the stress-strength parameter have received considerable attention and commonly used in many engineering applications. Let X and Y be two independent random variables showing the strength of a system and the stress applied to it, respectively, then R = P(Y < X) is the measure of the system performance which arises quite naturally in the mechanical reliability of a system. In this case the system fails if and only if the applied stress is larger than its strength at any time. In the statistical literature, several authors considered the estimation problem of the stress strength parameter. [2,3] studied the estimation of R, where X and Y are generalized exponential and Weibull random variables, respectively. [4] obtained the estimation of R, where X and Y are distributed as two independent three parameter generalized exponential random variables. [5] considered the estimation of R, where X and Y are two independent generalized Pareto distributions. In recent years, a many works have been done on the problem of estimating R of some distributions; See for example, [6][7][8][9][10][11][12][13][14] and [15]. These studies have actually considered the maximum likelihood and Bayesian estimation methods under different life testing schemes for various distributions. 

Many authors investigated the estimation of R = P(Y < X) when X and Y are independent Weibull random variables, see for example [3,7,[16][17][18], and see the references cited therein. These studies considered the maximum likelihood as a frequentist method as well as the Bayesian estimation method. But no much attention has been paid to use other frequentist methods to estimate R = P(Y < X), while in some cases they can provide better estimates than the maximum likelihood method. For this reason, our aim in this paper is to use nine frequentist methods of estimation besides the maximum likelihood estimation (MLE) method. In this paper, we focus on ten different estimation methods to estimate the stress-strength reliability and investigate how the different estimators behave for different sample sizes and for different parameter values.
</snippet>

Snippet: In this paper, we compared ten estimation methods of stress-strength parameter R = P(Y < X), when X and Y are two independent Weibull distributions with equal shape parameter. The methods are: the maximum likelihood, least square, weighted least square, percentile, maximum product of spacing, minimum spacing absolute distance, minimum spacing absolute-log distance, method of Crame ´r-von Mises, Anderson-Darling and Right-tail Anderson-Darling estimators. We also considered two parametric bootstrap confidence intervals of R, namely, the percentile bootstrap and bias corrected percentile bootstrap confidence intervals. The performance of the differenr estimators was compared by conducting an extensive Mont Carlo simulation study and via analysing one real data set. In presence of small samples the method of maximum product of spacing is perform better than the maximum likelihood method. Overall, the simulation results show that the percentile and maximum product of spacing methods perform better than the other methods in terms of minimum relative mean square error and confidence interval length in most of the cases. The bias corrected percentile bootstrap confidence intervals perform better than percentile bootstrap confidence intervals in terms of minimum confidence interval lengths. We recommend to use the maximum product of spacing methods to estimate the stress-strength parameter of the Weibull distributions especially when the sample size is small. A future work is to estimate R = P(Y < X) using the different estimation methods when the shape parameters are not the same. Another future work is to study and compare the Bayesian estimation based on maximum likelihood and based on maximum product of spacing to estimate the stress-strength reliability of Weibull distribution.

Title: Reliability of multi-component stress–strength models
Snippet: Estimation of the reliability of stress-strength models has been discussed in the literature extensively. For example Hanagal [1] obtained the estimation of the reliability of a series system under the assumption of a multivariate Pareto distribution for the strengths of the components and subjected to exponential common stress. Hanagal [2] obtained the estimation of system reliability of a stress-strength model with k components either parallel or series. He assumed that the distributions of the strengths of the k components and the distribution of the common stress are all independent and are two parameter exponential. Hanagal [3] obtained the estimation of system reliability in multi-component series stress-strength models. He considered the estimation of R ¼ P X kþ1 < minðX 1 ; X 2 ; Á Á Á ; X k Þ ð Þ when X i , i = 1,2,. . ., k + 1, all follow independent Gamma, Weibull and Pareto distributions. For the case of non-independent components, Hanagal [4] estimated the reliability of a parallel system with two components having a bivariate exponential distribution subjected to a common stress, which can be either exponential or gamma. Also Ba'akkel [5] discussed the reliability of a system with two components with strengths having a bivariate exponential distribution and subjected to different strategies of stresses. Ebrahimi [6] discussed series stress-strength models having bivariate Marshall-Olkin exponential strengths subjected to q stresses. The stresses are independent and exponentially distributed. 

Modern engineering systems may have more than two components. The components may fail separately or simultaneously. The (k + 1)-parameter multivariate exponential distribution and the absolutely continuous multivariate exponential (ACMVE) distribution may represent the lifetimes or strengths of such components. Hanagal [7] discussed the reliability of an s-out of k system. The strengths of the k-components follow the ACMVE distribution and are subjected to a common stress which is exponentially distributed. 

In some situations the system may be imposed to different stresses that could not be independent. Not too much work considered this case. In the present article, we consider the problem of estimating the reliability of a system with k components subjected to n stresses. The components could be arranged either parallel or series.

- k-out-of-n and mixed structures: R is expressed via order statistics or inclusion-exclusion over combinations, with estimators available under specific strength/stress families (e.g., Burr–XII) and progressively censored samples; parallel–series architectures combine these and have dedicated inference procedures and approximate confidence intervals <cite id="2f5b5454-2">Burr–XII-based k-out-of-n reliability in multicomponent stress–strength models has been estimated; parallel–series systems combine series and parallel at multiple levels and appear in power and aerospace; approximate confidence intervals and optimization designs exist; dependence between stress and strength is often realistic and should be modeled</cite><cite id="4fbe3d7a-0">Estimation for s-out-of-k systems has been extensively investigated for log-logistic, generalized exponential, Rayleigh, Burr Type XII, generalized Rayleigh, and Weibull/bivariate Kumarswamy cases</cite>. 
- General coherent structures: For arbitrary minimal cut-set/structure functions, reliability can be written as expectations over ordered strengths, enabling unified likelihood construction and numerical optimization; examples include Eryilmaz’s results for general coherent systems and for systems with dependent elements within units <cite id="2f5b5454-4">Eryilmaz studied stress–strength reliability for general coherent systems and for systems with n independent components each consisting of m dependent elements; Jae & Eun and Hanagal provided MLEs and MVUEs for specific coherent structures under Weibull and multivariate exponential models</cite>.

5) Advanced and dependent models
- Dependent strengths and stresses: Early work models multivariate exponential strengths (absolutely continuous or Marshall–Olkin) with independent or dependent stresses; more recent work explicitly incorporates dependence between stress and strength via copulas and multivariate families, which improves realism in environmental/operational settings <cite id="2f5b5454-0">Ebrahimi discussed series stress–strength models with bivariate Marshall–Olkin exponential strengths under independent exponential stresses; Hanagal treated dependent parallel systems with bivariate exponential strengths and common stress</cite><cite id="2f5b5454-2">Dependence between stress and strength is often induced by shared factors; parallel–series reliability studies emphasize that independence assumptions may be unrealistic, motivating dependence-aware estimation</cite>. 
- Copula-based and mixed-structure estimation: Copula frameworks and parallel–series decompositions allow flexible marginal modeling (e.g., Weibull, Rayleigh) with dependence captured by Hoeffding–Sklar copulas; inference uses MLE in the joint likelihood, bootstrap intervals, and Bayesian posterior sampling <cite id="ff6d9445-4">Stress–strength reliability has been studied under copula-based setups and progressively censored bivariate samples; methods include MLE, bootstrap intervals, and Bayesian estimation across exponential, Lindley, and Burr families</cite><cite id="2f5b5454-2">Copula-based reliability estimation has been applied to parallel–series systems in multicomponent stress–strength dependent models, enabling modular reliability aggregation with dependence</cite>. 
- Competing stresses or multiple stresses: Extensions estimate R for systems under multiple stresses with dependence, e.g., n stresses on k components arranged parallel or series; estimation proceeds by defining system failure events and optimizing the joint likelihood under multivariate exponential/Weibull families <cite id="2f5b5454-0">The article considers k components under n stresses with components arranged parallel or series, relaxing independence across stresses and accommodating dependence structures</cite>. 
- Load-sharing and dependent strengths within units: When components inside a unit share load (load-sharing), strength is a function of surviving components; Eryilmaz’s formulations address stress–strength reliability when n independent components each have m dependent elements, enabling estimation with MLE and MVUE under Weibull/exponential-type models <cite id="2f5b5454-4">Stress–strength reliability for systems with n independent components each consisting of m dependent elements was considered by Eryilmaz, with MLE and MVUE available; such load-sharing/dependent-element structures appear in engine, power, communication, and tire systems</cite>.

6) Data schemes, asymptotics, and intervals (practical tools)
- MLE is the default frequentist estimator when a closed-form likelihood exists; under regularity conditions, asymptotic normality of MLEs yields approximate confidence intervals via Fisher information, but simulations often show spacings-based and percentile/bias-corrected bootstrap intervals perform better in coverage and interval length for small to moderate samples <cite id="ff6d9445-2">For independent Weibull strengths and stresses, MLE and product-of-spacings were among top performers in RMSE and interval length; bias-corrected percentile bootstrap intervals were shortest on average</cite><cite id="ff6d9445-3">Percentile and maximum product-of-spacings methods were highly competitive across sample sizes; two parametric bootstrap intervals were compared</cite>. 
- Record-value and progressively censored schemes are common in reliability; estimators and intervals have been developed for these sampling schemes across exponential/Weibull/Burr families, using likelihood-ratio/score intervals and bootstrap <cite id="ff6d9445-1">Record-based Weibull stress–strength models admit MLE and Bayes estimators with bias/MSE analyses and likelihood/score/bootstrap confidence intervals plus HPD credible sets</cite><cite id="ff6d9445-4">Under progressive Type-II censoring, MLEs, asymptotic intervals, and bootstrap intervals have been derived for Burr XII; Lindley families admit consistent unbiased, MLE, Bayesian, and bootstrap estimation</cite>. 
- Specialized distributions and mixtures (e.g., generalized exponential/log-logistic/Rayleigh, Weibull–Rayleigh) support closed-form or numerically tractable likelihoods; approximate MLEs and simulation studies validate performance on real data <cite id="4fbe3d7a-0">Estimation under log-logistic, generalized exponential, Rayleigh, Burr Type XII, generalized Rayleigh, and Weibull/bivariate Kumarswamy families has been developed for multicomponent stress–strength models</cite><cite id="2f5b5454-1">Weibull–Rayleigh stress–strength reliability admits MLE and approximate MLE; two real data applications are provided</cite><cite id="ff6d9445-0">Generalized exponential and Weibull stress–strength reliability have been estimated via MLE and Bayesian methods with extensive reviews</cite>. 
- Unified likelihood and numerical optimization: For general coherent structures and s-out-of-k reliability expressed through order statistics, numerically stable likelihood evaluation with profile likelihood or EM-style algorithms yields point estimates and profile-based confidence intervals; Bayesian MCMC can sample the joint posterior over parameters and reliability <cite id="2f5b5454-4">Order-statistics expressions for multicomponent reliability enable MLE and MVUE under Weibull and multivariate exponential models; general coherent systems and dependent-element units have explicit estimators</cite><cite id="4fbe3d7a-4">Fully Bayesian estimation with UGG–Weibull strength/stress parameters can be implemented via joint posterior sampling over the eight-dimensional parameter vector</cite>.

7) Practical guidance and model selection
- Start by mapping the physical system to a reliability event: series/cold-standby uses the minimum strength exceeding stress; k-out-of-n uses the s-th order statistic threshold; parallel uses the maximum strength threshold; complex systems decompose into parallel–series or general coherent structures. Then select a family that fits stress and strength marginals (exponential/Weibull for monotone hazard, generalized families for heavy tails), and consider dependence via copulas if stress and strength are influenced by shared covariates or mechanisms <cite id="4fbe3d7a-2">System failure when stress exceeds the minimum component strength motivates series/cold-standby; s-out-of-k generalizes this; R = P(X > Y) is the single-component prototype</cite><cite id="2f5b5454-0">Hanagal and Ebrahimi’s treatments cover series/parallel/k-out-of-n under exponential, gamma/Weibull/Pareto, and multivariate exponential/Weibull families with and without dependence</cite><cite id="2f5b5454-2">Parallel–series architectures are widely used in critical infrastructure; dependence between stress and strength should be modeled when realistic</cite>. 
- Frequentist workhorse: MLE under the joint likelihood for the chosen family; compute profile likelihood or bootstrap intervals if closed-form quantiles are unavailable; favor product-of-spacings or percentile/bias-corrected bootstrap when samples are small and MLE is slightly biased <cite id="ff6d9445-2">MLE and product-of-spacings were top performers for R with independent Weibull strengths and stress</cite><cite id="ff6d9445-3">Bias-corrected percentile bootstrap yielded shorter intervals than percentile alone</cite>.

- Case library: s-out-of-k in power and telecom; engine/vehicle thermal-mechanical systems; multi-unit turbines or pumps; parallel–series power grids; wind farm turbine clusters. Each maps to an R expression in terms of order statistics and strengths/stresses; parameter estimation follows the general recipes above <cite id="2f5b5454-4">Examples include 4-out-of-8 engines, power stations with 6/8 units online, communication systems with 6/10 transmitters, and 6/8 tires; s-out-of-k is reviewed by Kuo & Zuo</cite>.

- Specify the system reliability expression R as an order-statistic probability P(Y < X_{(s)}), or a coherent-structure expectation; choose joint likelihood under appropriate marginals (e.g., Weibull, exponential, generalized families) and dependence structure (independence or copula/multivariate exponential); collect data (full, record, or progressively censored); then:
  - Frequentist: compute MLE (possibly profile), evaluate asymptotic variances or simulate bootstrap intervals; consider product-of-spacings and AD/CV MLE variants; benchmark RMSE and coverage on simulated data before applying to the field sample <cite id="ff6d9445-2">Ten frequentist estimators and two bootstrap intervals for R under Weibull with comparisons via simulation and a real data set</cite><cite id="ff6d9445-3">Product-of-spacings and bias-corrected bootstrap often yield best RMSE and interval lengths</cite><cite id="ff6d9445-1">Likelihood-based and bootstrap intervals with Bayes/MSE comparisons for Weibull record-based R</cite>.

The study of stress-strength model has received attention by the researchers because of its practical applications in the field of science and technology. The "stress-strength" reliability can be described as an assessment of reliability of a component in terms of random variable Y representing "stress" experienced by the component and X representing "strength" of a component available to overcome the possible stress, if the stress exceeds the strength, then the system will fail. The idea of stress-strength reliability R = P(X > Y) was introduced by Birnbaum [1] and developed by Birnbaum and McCarty [2]. Estimation of reliability in stress-strength model are considered in the literature when the stress and strength variables follow distributions such as exponential, Weibull, normal, gamma etc. Raqab et. al., [3] estimated the reliability of the model for a 3-parameter generalized exponential distribution. Wong [4] obtained confidence intervals for P(X > Y) when the underlying distribution is generalized Pareto. Angali et al. [5] considered Bayesian estimators of reliability for four parameter of bivariate exponential distribution under different loss functions. 

The estimation of multicomponent stress-strength reliability for s-out-of-k and the other related systems have been extensively investigated by many authors in the literature. An s-out-of-k system functions when the system having k statistically independent and identically distributed components functions if s (1 ≤ s ≤ k) or more components with stand a common stress, which was first studied by Bhattacharyya and Johnson [6]. This type of systems can be seen in both industrial and military applications [7]. Estimation of multicomponent stress-strength reliability is considered for the log-logistic, generalized exponential, generalized inverted exponential, Rayleigh, Burr Type XII and generalized Rayleigh distributions respectively by Rao and Kantam [8], Rao [9,10,11,12] and Rao et al. [13]. Pandit and Kantu [14] considered estimation of multicomponent stress-strength reliability for parallel and series systems when strength and stress variables follow exponential distribution.

Title: On estimation procedures of stress-strength reliability for Weibull distribution with application
Snippet: Since the pioneering work of Birnbaum [1], the statistical inference of the stress-strength parameter have received considerable attention and commonly used in many engineering applications. Let X and Y be two independent random variables showing the strength of a system and the stress applied to it, respectively, then R = P(Y < X) is the measure of the system performance which arises quite naturally in the mechanical reliability of a system. In this case the system fails if and only if the applied stress is larger than its strength at any time. In the statistical literature, several authors considered the estimation problem of the stress strength parameter. [2,3] studied the estimation of R, where X and Y are generalized exponential and Weibull random variables, respectively. [4] obtained the estimation of R, where X and Y are distributed as two independent three parameter generalized exponential random variables. [5] considered the estimation of R, where X and Y are two independent generalized Pareto distributions. In recent years, a many works have been done on the problem of estimating R of some distributions; See for example, [6][7][8][9][10][11][12][13][14] and [15]. These studies have actually considered the maximum likelihood and Bayesian estimation methods under different life testing schemes for various distributions. 

Many authors investigated the estimation of R = P(Y < X) when X and Y are independent Weibull random variables, see for example [3,7,[16][17][18], and see the references cited therein. These studies considered the maximum likelihood as a frequentist method as well as the Bayesian estimation method. But no much attention has been paid to use other frequentist methods to estimate R = P(Y < X), while in some cases they can provide better estimates than the maximum likelihood method. For this reason, our aim in this paper is to use nine frequentist methods of estimation besides the maximum likelihood estimation (MLE) method. In this paper, we focus on ten different estimation methods to estimate the stress-strength reliability and investigate how the different estimators behave for different sample sizes and for different parameter values.

Title: On estimation procedures of stress-strength reliability for Weibull distribution with application
Snippet: In this paper, we compared ten estimation methods of stress-strength parameter R = P(Y < X), when X and Y are two independent Weibull distributions with equal shape parameter. The methods are: the maximum likelihood, least square, weighted least square, percentile, maximum product of spacing, minimum spacing absolute distance, minimum spacing absolute-log distance, method of Crame ´r-von Mises, Anderson-Darling and Right-tail Anderson-Darling estimators. We also considered two parametric bootstrap confidence intervals of R, namely, the percentile bootstrap and bias corrected percentile bootstrap confidence intervals. The performance of the differenr estimators was compared by conducting an extensive Mont Carlo simulation study and via analysing one real data set. In presence of small samples the method of maximum product of spacing is perform better than the maximum likelihood method. Overall, the simulation results show that the percentile and maximum product of spacing methods perform better than the other methods in terms of minimum relative mean square error and confidence interval length in most of the cases. The bias corrected percentile bootstrap confidence intervals perform better than percentile bootstrap confidence intervals in terms of minimum confidence interval lengths. We recommend to use the maximum product of spacing methods to estimate the stress-strength parameter of the Weibull distributions especially when the sample size is small. A future work is to estimate R = P(Y < X) using the different estimation methods when the shape parameters are not the same. Another future work is to study and compare the Bayesian estimation based on maximum likelihood and based on maximum product of spacing to estimate the stress-strength reliability of Weibull distribution.

Title: On estimation procedures of stress-strength reliability for Weibull distribution with application
Snippet: For the first time, ten frequentist estimation methods are considered on stress-strength reliability R = P(Y < X) when X and Y are two independent Weibull distributions with the same shape parameter. The start point to estimate the parameter R is the maximum likelihood method. Other than the maximum likelihood method, a nine frequentist estimation methods are used to estimate R, namely: least square, weighted least square, percentile, maximum product of spacing, minimum spacing absolute distance, minimum spacing absolute-log distance, method of Cramér-von Mises, Anderson-Darling and Right-tail Anderson-Darling. We also consider two parametric bootstrap confidence intervals of R. We compare the efficiency of the different proposed estimators by conducting an extensive Mont Carlo simulation study. The performance and the finite sample properties of the different estimators are compared in terms of relative biases and relative mean squared errors. The Mont Carlo simulation study revels that the percentile and maximum product of spacing methods are highly competitive with the other methods for small and large sample sizes. To show the applicability and the importance of the proposed estimators, we analyze one real data set.

Title: Reliability of multi-component stress–strength models
Snippet: Estimation of the reliability of stress-strength models has been discussed in the literature extensively. For example Hanagal [1] obtained the estimation of the reliability of a series system under the assumption of a multivariate Pareto distribution for the strengths of the components and subjected to exponential common stress. Hanagal [2] obtained the estimation of system reliability of a stress-strength model with k components either parallel or series. He assumed that the distributions of the strengths of the k components and the distribution of the common stress are all independent and are two parameter exponential. Hanagal [3] obtained the estimation of system reliability in multi-component series stress-strength models. He considered the estimation of R ¼ P X kþ1 < minðX 1 ; X 2 ; Á Á Á ; X k Þ ð Þ when X i , i = 1,2,. . ., k + 1, all follow independent Gamma, Weibull and Pareto distributions. For the case of non-independent components, Hanagal [4] estimated the reliability of a parallel system with two components having a bivariate exponential distribution subjected to a common stress, which can be either exponential or gamma. Also Ba'akkel [5] discussed the reliability of a system with two components with strengths having a bivariate exponential distribution and subjected to different strategies of stresses. Ebrahimi [6] discussed series stress-strength models having bivariate Marshall-Olkin exponential strengths subjected to q stresses. The stresses are independent and exponentially distributed. 

Modern engineering systems may have more than two components. The components may fail separately or simultaneously. The (k + 1)-parameter multivariate exponential distribution and the absolutely continuous multivariate exponential (ACMVE) distribution may represent the lifetimes or strengths of such components. Hanagal [7] discussed the reliability of an s-out of k system. The strengths of the k-components follow the ACMVE distribution and are subjected to a common stress which is exponentially distributed. 

In some situations the system may be imposed to different stresses that could not be independent. Not too much work considered this case. In the present article, we consider the problem of estimating the reliability of a system with k components subjected to n stresses. The components could be arranged either parallel or series.

Title: On the Estimation of Stress Strength Reliability Parameter of Weibull-Rayleigh Distribution
Snippet: The reliability of a component depends on the stress conditions of the operating environment, which are uncertainty and should be modeled as random. This article deals with the estimation of the stress-strength reliability parameter of Weibull-Rayleigh distribution. Let X and Y be two independent random variables, where X and Y follow Weibull-Rayleigh distribution. The maximum likelihood estimator and the approximate maximum likelihood estimator of the stress-strength reliability are obtained. Other properties of the Weibull-Rayleigh distributions are derived. Two real data applications are given for showing the flexibility of the Weibull-Rayleigh stress-strength reliability.

Title: Copula-based reliability estimation of parallel-series system in the multicomponent stress–strength dependent model
Snippet: The study of multicomponent system reliability in stress-strength models holds significant value and provides meaningful insights. Eryilmaz [14] obtained the system reliability for a general coherent structure under stress-strength setup. Eryilmaz and Iscioglu [15] got some conclusions about stress-strength reliability in the context of multicomponent multi-state systems modeling. Reliability inference of k-out-of-n system for multicomponent stress-strength model under the assumptions of Burr-XII distribution was studied by [28]. Liu et al. [22] derived the reliability estimation of multicomponent system accounting for the stress-strength model and the specific N-M-cold-standby arrangement. Kohansal [20] focused on the estimation of system reliability for a k-out-of-n system within a multicomponent stress-strength model, employing progressively censored Kumaraswamy sample. The parallel-series system, an essential and widely used structure in reliability engineering, consists of several subsystems connected in parallel, each containing numerous components arranged in a series configuration, as illustrated in Figure 1. The parallel-series system is vital for ensuring high reliability, robust fault tolerance, and versatile operation, making it indispensable for critical applications like power grids, communication infrastructures, and aerospace technologies. For further studies on parallel-series systems, readers may refer to [26] and [2]. In the domain of reliability estimation for parallel-series systems, several researchers have proposed flexible methodologies. For instance, Coit [12] described a flexible procedure to establish approximate confidence interval (ACI) for system reliability in situations there is uncertainty about component reliability information. Empirical Bayesian variants further improve performance by estimating priors from data. <cite id="7d5446cb-0">Independent gamma priors with Gibbs–Metropolis sampling yield Bayes estimates and HPD credible intervals; performance is evaluated by simulation</cite><cite id="7d5446cb-1">Lindley’s approximation and MCMC compute Bayes estimates under squared error loss with gamma priors; HPD credible intervals are provided</cite><cite id="7d5446cb-2">Lindley’s and Tierney–Kadane approximations are used when explicit forms are lacking, with MCMC for credible intervals; a Monte Carlo comparison is carried out</cite><cite id="e2c25819-3">In s-out-of-k stress–strength with generalized Pareto under censoring and records, both frequentist and Bayesian procedures are assessed via detailed Monte Carlo to evaluate point and interval estimator properties</cite><cite id="7d5446cb-3">Empirical and full Bayesian estimators are compared for generalized Rayleigh stress–strength; comparisons are by MSE over large Monte Carlo samples and real data</cite>.

When to prefer which method

- Small-to-moderate samples: Prefer Bayesian estimation with reasonable priors (e.g., gamma on scale parameters under quadratic loss) to minimize MSE and ensure valid coverage; obtain credible intervals by MCMC or approximations (Lindley/Tierney–Kadane). <cite id="7d5446cb-1">Bayes estimates under squared error loss with gamma priors have smaller MSE than ML in Weibull s-out-of-k, with HPD credible intervals</cite><cite id="7d5446cb-2">Bayesian methods (Lindley, Tierney–Kadane, MCMC) are effective when explicit forms are lacking, with Monte Carlo comparison confirming performance</cite><cite id="7d5446cb-3">Empirical and full Bayesian approaches are compared via MSE in generalized Rayleigh models, with clear ordering of estimator performance</cite>.

- Alternative priors and loss: Objective/weakly informative priors (Jeffreys, reference, probability-matching) or robust loss can be tuned to the problem; simulation-based frequentist checks (MSE, coverage of HPD) remain essential. <cite id="e2c25819-0">For geometric stress–strength reliability, objective Bayesian priors (Jeffreys, reference, probability-matching) are developed and compared via RMSE and frequentist coverage of HPD credible intervals over Monte Carlo simulations</cite><cite id="e2c25819-4">Under generalized exponential–Poisson, estimators under eight loss functions are compared by MSE via simulation, with ordering of estimator performance</cite>.

Practical recommendations

- If you can specify a parametric family and obtain reasonable prior information, Bayesian estimation (MCMC or Lindley/Tierney–Kadane approximations) generally provides the most accurate reliability estimates in finite samples, measured by MSE and credible interval coverage; combine with RSS data collection for additional variance reduction. <cite id="7d5446cb-1">Bayes with gamma priors under quadratic loss yields smaller MSE than ML in Weibull s-out-of-k systems</cite><cite id="7d5446cb-2">Bayesian credible intervals via MCMC outperform asymptotic ML intervals in generalized Lindley stress–strength comparisons</cite><cite id="05e0e5c6-3">Ranked set sampling further reduces MSE relative to SRS in s-out-of-k reliability estimation</cite>.

- If priors are noninformative or unavailable, use ML for point estimation and assess interval accuracy with asymptotic or bootstrap intervals; in large samples, ML intervals will have near-target coverage and competitive MSE. <cite id="7d5446cb-0">Asymptotic ML intervals are standard and validated via simulation under Weibull joint censoring</cite><cite id="e2c25819-2">As sample size increases, ML MSE shrinks and approaches Bayes performance in MSE</cite>.

- For complex censoring/record designs, adopt censoring-aware likelihoods and simulation-based evaluation to ensure both point and interval estimators have desirable properties. <cite id="7d5446cb-0">Joint Type-II censoring models support ML and Bayesian estimation with simulation-based performance checks</cite><cite id="e2c25819-3">Monte Carlo studies evaluate estimator properties under block adaptive progressive hybrid censoring and k-records</cite>.

Limitations and caveats

- Misspecification of the stress–strength family or priors can hurt accuracy; robust checks (nonparametric/empirical Bayes, model selection) and simulation-based MSE/coverage diagnostics are essential. <cite id="7d5446cb-3">Empirical and full Bayesian methods are compared by MSE over large Monte Carlo studies to ensure robust performance</cite><cite id="e2c25819-0">Objective priors are evaluated via RMSE and coverage to mitigate prior sensitivity</cite>.

- Interval estimation nuances: asymptotic ML intervals can be anti-conservative under model misspecification or weak identifiability; HPD credible intervals from MCMC are model-dependent but calibrated via simulation. <cite id="7d5446cb-0">Asymptotic intervals are constructed from observed Fisher information; simulation studies compare with HPD credible intervals</cite><cite id="7d5446cb-2">MCMC credible intervals and ML asymptotic intervals are both implemented and compared in generalized Lindley models</cite>.

Bottom line

In large samples or with noninformative priors and strong identifiability, ML point estimates are asymptotically efficient, and ML-based asymptotic or bootstrap intervals achieve valid coverage, making them practically accurate and convenient. <cite id="7d5446cb-1">Bayes estimates under squared error loss with gamma priors have smaller MSE than ML in Weibull s-out-of-k systems</cite><cite id="7d5446cb-2">Bayesian credible intervals via MCMC/Lindley/Tierney–Kadane are effective and outperform asymptotic ML intervals in generalized Lindley comparisons</cite><cite id="e2c25819-2">For generalized Pareto, Bayes estimates under gamma priors have smaller MSE than ML, and RSS-based ML further reduces MSE relative to SRS</cite><cite id="05e0e5c6-3">Ranked set sampling yields preferred reliability estimates in generalized inverted exponential s-out-of-k systems compared to SRS</cite><cite id="7d5446cb-0">Asymptotic ML intervals and Bayesian HPD intervals are both evaluated by simulation under Weibull k-strength + 1-stress joint censoring</cite><cite id="e2c25819-1">ML and Bayesian estimators are compared via MSE and bias in record-based stress–strength reliability</cite><cite id="e2c25819-0">Objective priors and HPD credible intervals are assessed by RMSE and coverage in geometric stress–strength reliability</cite>.

Title: Reliability Estimation in Multicomponent Stress-Strength for Generalized Inverted Exponential Distribution Based on Ranked Set Sampling
Snippet: Highlights • This paper focuses on reliability estimation in a multicomponent stress-strength model. • Three sampling schemes are employed for estimation problem. • A simulation study is provided for illustrative purposes. Abstract Stress-strength models are considered of great significance due to their applicability in varied fields. We address the estimation of the system reliability of a multicomponent stress-strength model, say R s,k , of an s out of k system when the pair stress and strengths are drawn from a generalized inverted exponential distribution. The system is deemed as working if at least s out of k strengths be more than its stress. We obtain the reliability estimators when the data of strength and stress distributions are collected from three sampling schemes, specifically; simple random sampling, ranked set sampling, and median ranked set sampling. We obtain four estimators of R s,k out from median ranked set sampling. The behavior of different estimates is examined via a simulation study based on mean squared errors and efficiencies. The simulation studies point out that the reliability estimates of R s,k , from the ranked set sampling scheme are preferred than other estimates picked from the simple random sample and median ranked set sampling in a majority of the situations. The theoretical studies are explained with the aid of real data analysis.
